title: Better Ecommerce Inventory Tracking for Scaling Retailers
summary: Ecommerce inventory tracking fails when your stack is siloed. A headless, composable ERP unifies tools into a single source of truth, deploying in weeks.
body_text: Back to Resources ERP Retail Operations Better Ecommerce Inventory Tracking for Scaling Retailers Better Ecommerce Inventory Tracking for Scaling Retailers Inventory problems used to be addressed in an afternoon after a quick manual recount. But, as you’ve scaled your business, it’s likely that your inventory tracking have grown exponentially more complicated. Now, your old methods don’t quite work like they used to, and you’re getting bogged down by inventory emergencies, incorrect data, and slow reconciliation cycles. There’s a better way to handle your ecommerce inventory tracking, and it starts with your tech stack. Elijah MacDougall July 24, 2026 Want to test drive the most customizable ERP platform in the market? During your early days as a retailer, your ecommerce inventory tracking was simple: fewer SKUs, 1 or 2 storefronts to manage, and simple workflows to match. Inventory problems used to be addressed in an afternoon after a quick manual recount. But, as you’ve scaled your business, it’s likely that your inventory tracking have grown exponentially more complicated. Now, your old methods don’t quite work like they used to, and you’re getting bogged down by inventory emergencies, incorrect data, and slow reconciliation cycles. There’s a better way to handle your ecommerce inventory tracking, and it starts with your tech stack. What you’ll learn: The three ways your inventory tracking is going wrong Why your system isn’t set up to support accurate inventory tracking What headless, composable ERP can do to make your ecommerce inventory tracking scalable 3 Reasons Your Inventory Tracking Isn’t Quite Working For Your Retail Brand On a good week, your inventory numbers check out, and all systems are green — but there’s a catch. These “good” weeks are actually when your traffic is low or within expectations. Your actual “big picture” good weeks — when you’re managing rushes, huge orders, and exceeding sales projections — are fraught with emergency recounts, unexpected out-of-stock notices, and overselling inventory. As a scaling retailer, this state of affairs is unsustainable and prevents you from operating at peak efficiency. While these conditions are problematic, they don’t have to become the status quo. Before we identify some solutions, let’s explore the three main reasons your inventory tracking isn’t working for your business. System Visibility Is Siloed The first reason that your ecommerce inventory tracking might not be working for you is a problem that plagues many growing retail brands: system visibility. In the same way you might struggle to read a road sign in the early hours of a foggy morning, your inventory tracking software struggles to pull accurate data from other parts of your business. When your system visibility is low, it’s because the rest of your tech stack is siloed (or blocked off). Because your stack is blocked off, each part of your business is isolated, with each part operating in its own bubble. This breaks system cohesion and results in your tech stack having several points of fractured authority — or different batches of data claiming to have the truth about your inventory (without knowing what other parts of the system have). In order to fix this problem, you need to remove silos from your business and establish a single source of truth. Data Isn’t Flowing Properly A knock-on effect of having a siloed tech stack is that none of the data in your business flows as efficiently as it should. Ideally, a growing retailer would have a system where data is automatically reconciled by a single source of truth and automatically moved where it needs to go. Instead, retailers often end up with stagnant data that’s prone to errors caused by lagging reports and manually reconciling data in spreadsheets. Having to move data between parts of your tech stack with spreadsheets as a translation layer often results in a few major ecommerce inventory tracking issues: Transposed inventory numbers. This leads to discrepancies between actual inventory in the warehouse and what’s on the books. Lost data. When multiple people are working in one spreadsheet, the incident rate for accidentally deleted data goes up — creating opportunities for inventory tracking oversights. Slow system-wide reconciliation. Spreadsheets, while an invaluable and powerful tool, just aren’t meant to do system-wide inventory management. Because data needs to be copied to multiple software, reconciliation delays build up across your system. Operations Stalled by Disconnected Tools The final reason your ecommerce inventory tracking isn’t quite working for your business is that your tech stack and necessary tools aren’t fully connected to each other. They may have limited connections between a handful of tools, but they’re cut off from the rest of your tech stack. This results in having to create workarounds (which are often inefficient and prone to breaking), pay for expensive, custom translation layers, or, once again, rely on spreadsheets to fill the gaps across your business. When any of these temporary solutions break, it causes your day-to-day operations to stall — creating headaches for your Ops team. How Composable ERPs Wrangle Back Control of Your Inventory Management The problems that arise from low-performance inventory tracking solutions can spiral out of control quickly. Technical debt, crippling inventory issues, and organizational dysfunction can become a difficult wall to scale if left unchecked for too long. This is where a powerful, composable ERP integration like Tailor can help you wrangle control of your inventory tracking — while supporting the rest of your business. The benefits of a composable ERP for your ecommerce inventory tracking directly solve the problems explored earlier: Proper data flow aided by architectural improvements A fully connected tech stack supported by a single source of truth System flexibility provided by the removal of silos that blocked visibility Tailor accomplishes this through headless, composable design. Because it’s headless, you can adjust the backend system without impacting the frontend of the system (also referred to as a decoupled front and backend). This goes hand-in-hand with it being composable, because you can add new features or adjust existing functionality modularly — like building blocks. This results in a highly flexible, lightweight, and powerful system that brings your entire business together. Better System Architecture Improves Data Flow Tailor’s headless, composable ERP supports data delivery across your business by providing a series of architectural improvements: Real-time sync. By connecting every part of your business (including cloud and API-based tools), you’re able to keep data flowing across your business — without having to wait for reports or manually reconcile inventory numbers. Simplified workflows. When every part of your business is connected, and you no longer need to rely on workarounds to get things done, you can reduce your workflows down to their necessary steps — leading to faster task completion, quicker turnaround for your teams, and straightforward troubleshooting when things go wrong. End-to-End System Connections Boost Inventory Tracking The biggest impact that Tailor can have on your ecommerce inventory tracking is that it connects your entire tech stack end-to-end. In a system without a headless, composable ERP, visibility is low, and data flows slowly — requiring constant intervention to get it from point A to point B. However, with a composable system, visibility is at its highest; no silos in sight. Here’s what this looks like in practice: Tailor provides a single source of truth that dispels confusion with your ecommerce inventory tracking. Apps, software, and cloud tools you use every day have a centralized way to interface with each other, ensuring data gets where it needs to in real time. A connected system means that you can retire translation layers and spreadsheets that were causing problems in the first place. How Tailor’s Flexible System Helps You Scale At its core, Tailor is designed to help retail brands scale — fast. Whether you need an out-of-the-box UI with prebuilt modules that are ready for integration in weeks, or a flexible system that can be easily transformed by your technical team, Tailor’s system can meet your business where it’s at now, and grow with it for years to come. It’s not just the fast integration and modular design that make fast scaling possible. Our headless, composable ERP helps your retail brand scale by: Letting you set your pace. Each software you integrate influences how you operate. Some feature rigid UI and workflows that are hard to deal with, slowly contorting your business to fit the way these tools were designed to operate (often for the worse). With a headless, composable system, you can make your tools work for you. This means you can set your pace and scale at the rate you want. Keeping your options open. Older, rigid software — like some legacy ERP solutions — force you to grow in certain ways, regardless of whether it’s the right call for your business. However, when your business is built on a composable foundation, you can keep your operations flexible. This enables you to grow exactly how you want and easily branch into new markets when you’re ready. Providing a shield against market chaos. When you don’t have the right tools in your business, you can get stuck in reactivity loops caused by market chaos (or unexpected events that threaten the way you’ve been operating). Something breaks, and you’re spending all your time fixing it. With composability at the heart of your system, you can take the chaos in stride without getting derailed. Composability’s Secret Ingredient for Sustainable Business Growth Along with all the benefits and improvements we discussed, there’s a secret ingredient that makes a headless, composable ERP so powerful for scaling retail brands: API & AI connectivity. Tailor uses APIs to bring your disconnected tools together and provide a single source of truth. Because you can interface with all your tools in a single screen, you can get the most out of their functionality, without convoluted workflows. By being AI-native, Tailor is able to integrate AI-powered tools and powerful AI workflows into your business without them feeling bolted-on — preparing your business to remain on the cutting edge. Take Control of Your Ecommerce Inventory Tracking The good news is: your ecommerce inventory tracking can work better for the way your business operates today and in the future. While it’s unlikely that you’ll go back to the simplicity of your early days of inventory tracking, you can make it far easier (and more accurate) than it has been. The change starts with embracing composable software. By removing the complexity caused by a disconnected system, with poor data flow and low system visibility, you can speed up your entire business, simplify your day-to-day operations, and make your ecommerce inventory tracking something you don’t need to worry about. Book a demo with us today to see how our headless, composable ERP, out-of-the-box usable UI, and inventory module can get your retail business scaling faster than ever in just a few weeks. title: Best Sales Tools in 2026: Top Picks for Every Funnel Stage
summary: The best sales tools for 2026 across every funnel stage-prospecting, outreach, CRM, analytics and closing. Compared on features, pricing and best use.
body_text: The best sales tools in 2026 cover every stage of the funnel — prospecting, outreach, scheduling, conversation intelligence, CRM and closing — and the right stack is the one that covers each stage without overlap. This guide organizes the top tools by what they do, gives current pricing, and shows how to build a lean stack. (For AI-specific tools, see our AI sales tools guide ; for data and lead sourcing, the lead generation tools roundup .) Key takeaways A complete sales stack spans six jobs: prospecting, outreach, scheduling, conversation intelligence, CRM and proposals . Most teams need only 3–6 core tools — coverage of each stage matters more than tool count. Match tools to your funnel gaps, not to hype; tool sprawl wastes budget and fragments data. An agentic AI sales agent can consolidate the prospecting-and-outreach stages into one autonomous workflow. Apollo — a large contact database plus sequencing, with a free tier; the best budget all-in-one for SMB prospecting. ZoomInfo — the enterprise data standard, with the largest verified database and intent signals (quote-based). LinkedIn Sales Navigator — the default for social prospecting (~$99/mo). For a full data-tool comparison, see the lead generation tools roundup . Best outreach & engagement tools This is where outbound happens — sequencing, personalization and follow-up across channels. Floworks (Alisha) — an agentic AI sales agent that researches, personalizes, sends and follows up automatically. Best when the bottleneck is doing outreach at scale, not just sending it. Salesloft / Outreach — the enterprise engagement platforms for managing multichannel cadences at scale (quote-based). Lemlist — creative, personalized email plus LinkedIn steps, from ~$39/mo. For outbound strategy, see our B2B outbound sales guide . Best scheduling tools Calendly — frictionless booking with time-zone handling and reminders (free; paid from ~$10/mo). Chili Piper — instant lead routing and round-robin booking for inbound demos (quote-based). Best conversation intelligence tools Gong — records and analyzes calls to surface deal risk, objections and coaching insights (quote-based). Fathom — lightweight AI meeting summaries and action items (free; premium from ~$15/mo). Best CRM tools HubSpot — the most user-friendly all-in-one CRM with strong automation (free; paid from ~$20/seat/mo). Salesforce — the most customizable enterprise CRM (from ~$25/seat/mo). Pipedrive — a simple, pipeline-focused CRM for SMBs (from ~$14.90/seat/mo). For automating your CRM, see CRM automation . Best proposal & closing tools PandaDoc — proposals, quotes and e-signatures with engagement tracking (from ~$19/mo). DocuSign — the e-signature standard for contracts (from ~$10/mo). How to build your sales stack You don’t need 15 tools — you need coverage of each stage without overlap. A practical approach: Start with a CRM as the system of record (HubSpot, Salesforce or Pipedrive). Add a prospecting/data tool and an outreach tool to fill the top of funnel. Add scheduling to remove booking friction. Layer in conversation intelligence and proposals as you scale. Audit for overlap. If two tools do the same job, cut one — sprawl fragments data and wastes budget. Many teams now consolidate the prospecting-and-outreach stages into a single agentic AI sales agent , reducing the number of point tools to manage. Frequently asked questions What are the best sales tools in 2026? It depends on the funnel stage: Apollo and ZoomInfo for prospecting, Floworks and Salesloft for outreach, Calendly for scheduling, Gong for conversation intelligence, HubSpot and Salesforce for CRM, and PandaDoc for proposals. Most teams build a stack of 3–6 tools across these stages. How many sales tools does a team need? Usually 3–6 core tools — typically a CRM, a prospecting/data tool, an outreach tool and a scheduling tool, plus conversation intelligence and proposals as you scale. Aim for coverage of each stage without overlap. How much does a sales tech stack cost? Entry tools start free to ~$50/user/mo; a mid-market stack runs $100–$500/user/mo; enterprise platforms are quote-based. Verify current pricing before budgeting. What’s the difference between a sales tool and an AI sales agent? Most sales tools assist a human with one task — finding a contact, sending a sequence, booking a meeting. An agentic AI sales agent runs the whole top-of-funnel motion autonomously: researching, personalizing, sending and following up. Cover the funnel without the tool sprawl The best stack is the leanest one that covers every stage. Consolidating prospecting and outreach into one agentic workflow is the fastest way to simplify it. body_text: View All News Nayax: Information Security Incident Update July 14, 2026 HERZLIYA, Israel, July 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Further to Nayax’s announcement dated July 8, 2026, regarding a suspected information security incident, the Company provides the following update. The Company's system review and technical remediation activities have been completed, and the Company's systems have been cleared and based on its investigation to date, confirmed to be free of unauthorized access. The Company's production environment and core systems have not been impacted. The Company's business operations continue as normal, without disruption or impact on our operations. As the Company's investigation progressed, and while the precise scope and complete contents of the exfiltrated information are still under investigation, findings have emerged indicating that such exfiltrated information includes a copy of a backup of scanned documents, additional business-related information, and mainly back up of payment transaction records which does not include sensitive payment authentication data (such as cardholder names, CVV values or ID information), as such information is generally not retained within the Company's systems. In addition, a significant portion of the transactions were conducted using digital wallets, such as Apple Pay and Google Pay, in which the payment credentials consist of single-use tokens that have no value if disclosed. Based on its investigation to date, the Company confirms that all customer safeguarded funds were untouched and that no unauthorized access to those accounts occurred. The Company's Board of Directors has resolved not to comply with criminal extortion demands. The Board believes that complying with such demands would not be consistent with the long-term best interests of the Company's customers, partners, employees and shareholders. The Company has incurred, and may continue to incur, costs related to responding to, remediating, and investigating this attack. The full financial impact-including insurance or indemnification offsets and any effect on customer behavior-is not yet determined, but the Company does not currently expect a material effect on its financial condition or results of operations. The Company continues to cooperate fully and closely with the relevant law enforcement authorities, which continue to conduct an intensive investigation into the incident and those responsible. ABOUT NAYAX Nayax is a global commerce enablement, payments and loyalty platform designed to help merchants scale their business. Nayax offers a complete solution including localized cashless payment acceptance, management suite, and loyalty tools, enabling merchants to conduct commerce anywhere, at any time. With foundations and global leadership in serving unattended retail, Nayax has transformed into a comprehensive solution focused on our customers' growth across multiple channels. As of March 31, 2026, Nayax has 13 global offices, approximately 1,250 employees, connections to more than 80 merchant acquirers and payment method integrations and is globally recognized as a payment facilitator. Nayax's mission is to improve our customers' revenue potential and operational efficiency, effectively and simply. For more information, please visit www.nayax.com . title: How to Migrate Off Medallia or Qualtrics Without Losing Your Feedback History
summary: A playbook to switch your feedback analytics off Medallia or Qualtrics without losing history: export, layer on top, re-analyze, then run in parallel.
body_text: Switching your feedback analytics off Medallia or Qualtrics feels risky for one reason: the history. Years of themed feedback, a taxonomy your team built by hand, and trend lines your executives watch every quarter all seem to live inside the tool you want to leave. Lose those and you start over blind. You do not have to. The way to migrate without losing your history is to treat it as a phased switch, not a rip-and-replace: export your raw data and your analytics tags, layer the new platform on top of your existing collection first, re-analyze your full history in the new tool so the trend lines stay continuous, then run both systems in parallel until the numbers reconcile. Thematic is built for exactly this path. It sits on top of Medallia, Qualtrics, and your data warehouse, imports historical feedback, and re-analyzes it under one taxonomy so your history carries forward intact. Below is the seven-step process, a worked example, and the mistakes that cause teams to lose history they did not need to lose. The migration in seven steps Time the switch to your renewal window. Start 90 to 120 days before auto-renewal so you have leverage and no gap. Inventory your current program before you touch anything. Every survey, dashboard, alert, integration, and text-analytics model, each with a named owner. Export your raw data and your analytics tags, not PDF dashboards. Tags are often not portable by default, so pull them out deliberately. Layer the new analytics on top of your existing collection first. Keep collecting where you collect today; switch the analysis layer. Re-analyze your history so the trend lines stay continuous. Import the full back catalog of feedback and re-theme it under one taxonomy. Run both systems in parallel and validate before cutover. Reconcile scores and theme volumes old versus new against a set threshold. Cut over, retire the old analytics, and bring stakeholders with you. Move reports on a schedule people know about, not overnight. Step 1: Time the switch to your renewal window Start the migration 90 to 120 days before your contract auto-renews. This is the window where you have both leverage and time. Leverage, because a renewal decision is the one moment the incumbent is motivated to help you export cleanly. Time, because a proper migration for an enterprise program runs weeks, not days, and you never want to be mid-cutover with the old contract already lapsed. Use this window to confirm your exit terms in writing. Gartner has long advised organizations to negotiate data-extraction and transition rights into SaaS contracts, and to budget the full cost of leaving, including a period of running two systems in parallel. If your current contract is silent on data export, that is a finding to resolve now, not at cutover. Step 2: Inventory your current program before you touch anything You cannot migrate what you have not mapped. Before any data moves, build an inventory of everything your current platform does: every live survey, every dashboard, every alert rule, every downstream integration, and every text-analytics model or code-frame. Give each one a named owner. This inventory is what protects your history. Most migrations lose data not because export is hard but because no one wrote down that a quarterly board dashboard depended on a specific theme that lived only in the old tool. The teams that switch cleanly treat the inventory as the migration's source of truth and check every item off at cutover. Step 3: Export your raw data and your analytics tags, not PDF dashboards Export two things: the raw feedback responses, and the analytics layer built on top of them (themes, tags, sentiment, code-frames). A PDF dashboard is a picture of your history, not your history. You cannot re-query it, and you cannot carry its trends into a new platform. The tags matter as much as the raw text, because analytics tags are frequently not portable by default. Qualtrics' own documentation notes that Text iQ topics do not transfer during a user move: you have to export the topics first and re-import them afterward. Assume the same of any incumbent. Pull your raw responses and your tag data out in a queryable format such as CSV or JSON, so the new platform can read both. Step 4: Layer the new analytics on top of your existing collection first Switching your analytics platform does not require ripping out the tool you collect feedback with. In most cases you should not. The survey platform, the app-store feed, the support desk: those can stay. What you are replacing is the analytics layer that reads the feedback and turns it into themes. Thematic connects to Medallia, Qualtrics, and warehouses like Snowflake or BigQuery natively or through an API, and analyzes the feedback that flows through them. A New Zealand vehicle-glass repair company kept its existing Qualtrics survey collection and Power BI reporting , and layered Thematic on top to discover themes and tie them to net promoter score (NPS) impact. There was no rip-and-replace of the survey stack. Layering first also de-risks the move: you prove the new analytics on live data before you touch anything upstream. Step 5: Re-analyze your history so the trend lines stay continuous This is the step that actually preserves your history, and the one most migration guides skip. Exporting your old data keeps it. Re-analyzing it makes it usable. Import the full back catalog of feedback into the new platform and re-theme all of it under one taxonomy, so a trend line that starts three years ago continues unbroken through the cutover. Thematic imports historical feedback and analyzes it alongside new feedback, and when a theme changes it re-analyzes all existing feedback so historical trends stay consistent and comparable. Map your old code-frames to the new themes as part of this step. The goal is that the taxonomy you spent years building is carried forward and improved, not abandoned, and that no executive opens a dashboard after cutover to find the history starts at zero. Step 6: Run both systems in parallel and validate before cutover Do not cut over on faith. Run the old platform and the new one side by side for a defined overlap window, feeding both the same feedback, and reconcile their output. Compare the headline scores, such as NPS or customer satisfaction (CSAT), and the volumes of your major themes, old system versus new. Set an acceptance threshold in advance and only cut over when the new platform's numbers reconcile with the old within it. This validation step is what turns a scary switch into a defensible one. When a skeptical stakeholder asks whether the new numbers can be trusted, the answer is a reconciliation report, not a shrug. Parallel running is a recognized, budgetable part of a proper migration, not wasted overhead. Step 7: Cut over, retire the old analytics, and bring stakeholders with you Once the parallel period validates, cut over on a schedule everyone knows about. Migrations rarely fail on the technology. They fail when a report moves under someone without warning and trust evaporates. Announce the cutover date, show each stakeholder where their dashboard now lives, and keep the old system readable for a short grace period. Then retire the incumbent analytics, or downgrade it to a collection-only role if you are keeping its survey capability. You are not just turning off a tool. You are moving your team onto one where the themes are theirs to edit and every conclusion traces back to the comments behind it. A worked example Atlassian ran into the problem this playbook solves at scale. Feedback was arriving across many channels, and manual reporting took six weeks, which is too slow to act on. The team evaluated 36 vendors before choosing Thematic, then connected its sources through an API into one shared taxonomy with deduplication, so the same theme meant the same thing across every channel. About 60,000 pieces of feedback a month flowed through that single analytics layer, and reporting that had taken six weeks moved to real time. The collection sources did not have to be torn out; the analytics layer on top of them changed. The payoff of getting the switch right shows up in analyst time. Vodafone New Zealand moved off manual, labor-intensive categorization of its NPS verbatims and onto automated analysis in Thematic. The team saved 60 hours every month and posted a double-digit increase in transactional NPS (tNPS) over nine months once it could act on what the feedback was actually saying. Common mistakes to avoid Exporting PDF dashboards instead of raw data and tags. A PDF is a snapshot, not queryable history. Pull the raw responses and the tag and theme data. Ripping out your collection layer when you only needed to switch analytics. Keep collecting where you collect today; replace the layer that reads and themes the feedback. Cutting over with no parallel-run validation. Without reconciling old and new scores and theme volumes, you have no way to prove the new numbers are right. Not mapping your old taxonomy. If legacy code-frames are not mapped to the new themes, your trend lines break exactly at the cutover, which is the history you were trying to protect. Treating it as a purely technical project. The failure mode is organizational: stakeholders blindsided by moved reports. Communicate the cutover before it happens.
